title: Artifact byte checksums
text: API: md5 gives the exact contract. artifact_checksum::md5 computes the sixteen MD5 digest bytes for a byte slice. The artifact parser uses this legacy checksum for its Z-card check. The Z card is the artifact checksum record. It does not select repository content identities. SHA-1 and SHA3 remain in content_hash. Structural parsing has its own explicit limits and validation rules. Md5Checksum::new starts an owned computation. update appends the complete slice, including zero bytes and bytes outside UTF-8. Empty updates do nothing. finish consumes the computation and returns [u8; 16]. Each value has fixed memory use and can be interleaved with other computations. No input copy, file access or process-global state is required. Slice lengths bound each call. The caller chooses how much data to supply. There is no artifact size policy or cancellation mechanism in this byte primitive. use gossil::artifact_checksum::{md5, Md5Checksum}; let mut checksum = Md5Checksum::new(); checksum.update(b"a"); checksum.update(b"bc"); assert_eq!(checksum.finish(), md5(b"abc"));

title: Artifact byte checksums
text: The inspected Fossil mirror is b3a1c8efb2731dffbd5cc38c58ac349746de6da6. The native build reports 7e8ecf0ce4a3c05aa39de7ffe2828d23e334efe446ef2387e09f205ef00b2227. In src/manifest.c, verify_z_card hashes the bytes before the final 35-byte Z card through md5sum_init, md5sum_step_text and md5sum_finish. This module supplies that checksum operation. It does not inspect a Z card. The byte result maps to md5sum_blob in src/md5.c. The incremental operations map to the positive-length and zero-length byte behavior of md5sum_step_text. Rust ownership replaces the native shared context and overwritten static result. The consuming finish requires a fresh value for another computation. It does not reproduce the native implicit reset. Negative lengths and C string scanning are excluded. md5sum_step_blob needs no separate Rust adapter because slices already describe bytes and length. Excluded native functions are md5sum_current_state, md5sum_file and md5sum_test. md5sum_current_state sums words of the internal context for troubleshooting. Its two callers in vfile.c are commented out. It is not a snapshot of the MD5 digest. The native command and filesystem behaviors, repository R-card aggregation, ETags and all artifact producers remain outside this module. Native MD5Init, MD5Update, MD5Final, MD5Transform and DigestToBase16 are not translated into Rust here. The implementation uses RustCrypto’s exact-pinned md-5 version 0.10.6. This version shares the existing digest 0.10 dependency with SHA-2. The lockfile records its registry checksum. Its versioned documentation describes the API used here. RustCrypto’s current documentation identifies legacy interoperability as the purpose of MD5. This module adds no identity or security policy and forwards no computation to C.

title: Artifact parser
text: API: parse_artifact and parse_artifact_with_usage give the exact contracts. The artifact module parses all eight Fossil structural artifact types with explicit resource limits. The types are manifest, cluster, control, wiki, ticket, attachment, technote and forum. A card is a record in the artifact byte format. The parser takes bytes and returns an owned result with read-only access to parsed fields. It keeps the original input, including any signature envelope. It does not require valid UTF-8.

title: Artifact parser
text: Call parse_artifact(input, limits, dates).await with a ParseLimits value chosen for the calling operation. Set each field explicitly, including input_bytes, cards, owned_bytes and entries. All four fields have type usize. The byte fields count bytes, and the other fields count cards and list entries. There is no default policy. The owned-byte limit counts logical charges for retained input, encoded tokens, copies and list entries. Allocations use fallible reservation. A resource failure is separate from malformed input, checksum mismatch and a date-provider failure.

title: Artifact parser
text: For several artifacts in one operation, call parse_artifact_with_usage(input, limits, dates).await. It returns the same parsed result with a ParseUsage value on success. The original parse_artifact function delegates to this implementation and returns only the parsed result. ParseUsage reports the existing limit counters. input_bytes counts the full raw input, including a recognized signature envelope. cards counts nonzero card markers consumed by the structural loop, including Z and repeated empty P cards. A trailing zero marker consumes its delimiter without adding a card. Body newlines and envelope lines do not add cards. owned_bytes reports all charged bytes, including retained raw input, copies, encoded token lengths charged before decoding, and the size of inserted list entries. The counters report logical charges against ParseLimits; they do not measure every physical Rust allocator byte. This charge can exceed the decoded output length. It also includes allocations for tokens later discarded, such as reserved file paths. entries counts list insertions; empty P cards add none. Subtract successful usage from the operation’s remaining limits before the next call. Each call checks those remaining limits before its charged allocations. Usage is returned only on success. A caller that needs an atomic operation must stop on any error and discard its operation state. The parser does not maintain the aggregate budget or remember earlier failures. The API example parses a cluster and subtracts all four successful charges from a caller-owned budget. Aggregate caller integration remains separate work.

title: Artifact parser
text: Implement DateProvider on the operation’s selected SQLite/libSQL owner. Its asynchronous julianday method can borrow a transaction. It receives an optional raw token already truncated by the parser at its native C-string boundary, and returns an optional Julian day. A NULL result acts as zero and fails date validation. Provider execution errors retain their original cause. A constant date adapter can isolate grammar tests, but it cannot qualify date compatibility. The result exposes decoded comments and users, manifest files and parents, tags, ticket fields and cluster members. It also exposes attachment fields, wiki and forum fields, body bytes and converted dates. D cards carry artifact dates, and E cards carry event dates. Their raw date tokens remain available. Callers cannot construct or mutate a validated result through this API.

title: Artifact parser
text: The port follows Fossil manifest.c:467-1153 and its eight allowed/required card masks at lines 129-138. The pinned Fossil UUID is 7e8ecf0ce4a3c05aa39de7ffe2828d23e334efe446ef2387e09f205ef00b2227. Fossil’s source is copyright D. Richard Hipp under the Simplified BSD License. The parser checks the exact MD5 before decoding a recognized final Z record. It strips recognized PGP and SSH envelopes for parsing and checksum purposes. Envelope stripping does not verify a signature’s authenticity. The pinned card matrix requires Z even for manifests. R validates hexadecimal syntax. Repository file checksum verification belongs to storage. Tokens stop at space, LF or raw NUL. Each card consumes tokens as its native branch does. A raw NUL can be an intermediate delimiter in some cards. It is not subject to a blanket acceptance rule. Decoded tokens retain bytes after an escaped NUL, together with the length visible to C consumers. A zero card marker ends the native card loop after consuming its space or LF delimiter. Parsing succeeds only if that cursor reaches the end and the earlier cards satisfy the type rules. Unread bytes after the marker still fail. The W scanner uses unsigned 32-bit modular arithmetic and the native new < old overflow branch. It checks the remaining input before copying body bytes. Decimal suffixes and empty digit sequences follow the source branch. Manifest file paths use the legacy nonstrict rules. Paths must be nonempty and have no empty, dot or dot-dot slash-separated components. Unicode and backslash restrictions are not imposed. Reserved filenames are suppressed after comparison with the last retained filename. The parser retains repeated empty P cards, native type inference, tag ordering, forum postconditions and the historical technote P-before-N exception. Attachment basenames follow the compiled platform’s directory separator rule. Windows behavior remains unqualified.

title: Byte digests and packed blobs
text: API: pack gives the exact contract. The library has Fossil byte digests and packed-blob operations. Packing adds a capacity header to compressed bytes. These primitives do not select a repository hash policy or store content. The runner and these primitives share a crate. CLI integration remains separate work. Legacy MD5 checksums have a separate artifact checksum module. The artifact parser uses that module for Z-card validation. The checksum module does not select repository content identities.

title: Byte digests and packed blobs
text: use gossil::{compression, content_hash}; let digest = content_hash::sha1(b"abc"); assert_eq!(digest.len(), 20); let packed = compression::pack(b"abc", -1).unwrap(); assert_eq!(compression::unpack(&packed, 3).unwrap(), compression::Unpacked::Bytes(b"abc".to_vec())); In the example, -1 selects the default compression level, and 3 limits decoded output to three bytes. sha1(input: &[u8]) returns [u8; 20]. pack(input: &[u8], level: i32) returns Result , BlobError>. unpack(input: &[u8], max_output: usize) returns Result . See the runner prerequisites for actual tool setup.

title: Byte digests and packed blobs
text: The port follows Fossil Git revision b3a1c8efb2731dffbd5cc38c58ac349746de6da6. The source surfaces are src/blob.c:1372–1535, src/sha1.c:185–201, and src/sha3.c:385–468,591–606,622–679, and the SHA1DC initialization in src/sha1hard.c:1327–1342. content_hash::sha1 accepts arbitrary bytes and returns twenty digest bytes. SHA1DC detects known SHA1 collision attacks. It preserves Fossil’s collision detection and safe-hash defaults. For a known collision attack, it returns the mitigated digest. The byte helper ignores the separate collision indication, as sha1sum_blob does. It does not return the ordinary vulnerable digest for those inputs. content_hash::sha3 accepts each width from 128 through 512 in steps of 32. It returns the corresponding binary digest, or None for an unsupported width. content_hash::hex renders bytes as lowercase hexadecimal. SHA3 uses Fossil’s width-dependent capacity and its 0x06 and 0x80 padding. The small adapter handles byte absorption, padding and extraction in explicit little-endian lane order. The maintained keccak crate supplies the permutation. A shorter digest is not a truncated standard-width hash. The four standard widths use FIPS-202 padding. The other widths preserve Fossil’s extensions. compression::pack accepts zlib levels -1 and zero through nine. Level -1 selects the backend default. compression::pack_two compresses the concatenated slices at level nine, as Fossil does. Neither operation allocates a concatenated input buffer. The compressed representation can differ between backends. A packed blob contains a four-byte unsigned big-endian capacity followed by a zlib stream. The capacity is an upper bound on decoded bytes. A larger header than the actual output is valid. Bytes following the first complete zlib stream are ignored. Invalid checksums, incomplete streams and output exceeding the header produce errors. compression::unpack accepts a caller-selected limit. It rejects a header above that limit before decoding, then checks each output chunk against the header. Output grows through fallible reservations. The caller sets the limit. The format has no additional fixed small cap. Encoding rejects lengths above the unsigned 32-bit header range. C overflow and undefined behavior are not ported. Inputs of at most four bytes produce Unpacked::NoPayload. A caller that replaces an existing buffer must leave its existing buffer contents unchanged for that result. A successfully decoded empty stream produces Unpacked::Bytes with an empty vector. These outcomes differ. Fossil’s diagnostic test-uncompress ignores the C function’s error return, so CLI exit zero does not prove successful decoding. Allocation and compression errors retain their underlying causes. Digest results have a fixed small size. Compressed input and output remain caller-owned. The API does not define database, filesystem, publication or privacy behavior.

title: CLI reference
text: The gossil executable initializes empty repositories and has three file diagnostics. Each diagnostic runs without a repository. Run it from this source checkout with just gossil, which builds and runs the executable through Cargo. Cargo may print build messages on stderr. Command Arguments Successful output vcs test-delta-create ORIGIN TARGET DELTA Writes DELTA; no stdout vcs test-delta-apply ORIGIN DELTA TARGET Writes TARGET; no stdout vcs test-delta FILE1 FILE2 Prints ok and a newline just gossil vcs test-delta-create ORIGIN TARGET DELTA just gossil vcs test-delta-apply ORIGIN DELTA TARGET just gossil vcs test-delta FILE1 FILE2 Replace capitalized arguments with file paths. The commands accept exactly the number of paths shown. Each diagnostic requires the vcs or v group. Neither executable has help subcommands. File data comes from paths and goes to paths. Stdin and stdout do not carry it.

title: CLI reference
text: just gossil vcs init --admin-user alice --date-override '2026-11-18 12:34:56' NEW_REPOSITORY just gossil vcs new --sha1 ANOTHER_NEW_REPOSITORY Initialization accepts exactly one destination. Both executable names and both group names support init and its new alias. The destination must be new; existing files, symlinks and SQLite recovery sidecars are refused. Option Behavior --admin-user USERNAME, -A USERNAME Set the initial administrator --date-override DATETIME Set the root date; default now --sha1 Use SHA1 for the initial root and native hash policy --help, -h Print initialization help and exit successfully -- Treat following arguments as literal destination names Long value options also accept --name=value. Without an explicit administrator, the command selects the first nonempty value from GOSSIL_USER, USER, LOGNAME and USERNAME, in that order. If all are absent or empty, it uses root. No preference file is read or created. Administrator bytes reach native validation unchanged; the storage API requires valid UTF-8. Repository filenames retain native bytes, including names beginning with file:. Dates must be UTF-8 and accepted by the native date provider. The receipt prints the committed project and server identifiers, administrator and initial remote-access password. Keep that password private. A receipt write failure returns status 1 after commit and leaves the repository initialized. Other initialization failures also return status 1. Initialization help returns 0. The command creates an empty native root without a checkout. Templates, project display fields and global preference options are unsupported and rejected before creation. Checkout registration, file recording and history commands remain planned. This source interface is separate from the existing default mini-VCS preview; this guide does not record a new installation or publication.

An output-open failure reports unable to open file "PATH" for writing. Invalid delta application reports Delta application failed.. A failed round trip reports delta test failed. Create and apply read their inputs before opening the output. This permits an output path to name an input file. Input or validation failures preserve an existing output, but an output write failure can leave it truncated. Parent folders must already exist. title: Compare Gossil with Git
text: Gossil is designed to keep agent files, typed issues and their connections to code in one coordinated history alongside Git. A historical view selects an exact file head, complete issue and discussion boundaries, and versioned links between issues and code. Git remains the source-code authority. This page compares that intended design with Git’s available behavior. The source CLI initializes empty repositories without a checkout and offers three delta diagnostics. The Rust library provides typed task, project and author converters, a task artifact emitter, and native storage primitives. It does not yet create or read persisted issues. Issue commands, checkout registration and file recording remain planned in this source CLI. See the current limits and CLI reference before trying a command.

title: Compare Gossil with Git
text: In Git, the working tree contains the files you edit. The index is the staging area for the next commit. Normally, a commit records the index as a file tree, with parents and a message. You can stage selected changes before committing; a commit need not include every edit on disk. See the Git tutorial and commit reference. Git can version task documents, plans and evidence in that same tree. Branches and commit history support many ways to organize the work. Git notes can attach information to an object without changing that object; notes have their own references and history. See Git notes. Need Git Intended Gossil design Record selected files Commits retain trees selected through the index or commit options Native file check-ins retain explicitly tracked agent files Record a task Version a task document or use a chosen tracker and integration Typed project/task records have defined fields, identities and reconstruction rules Select an earlier review state Name commits and any separately required task or notes history Select the file head plus complete exact boundaries for issues, links and discussions Connect an issue to code Adopt conventions or tools for references and reverse lookup Version typed links to registered Git repositories and support lookup in both directions Coordinate related changes A commit can include code and task documents in one tree One local database transaction coordinates selected Gossil files, records, scope and checkout heads Keep private agent material Choose a repository layout and sharing policy Keep private and shared material within one repository, with an explicit internal boundary A standalone tracker beside Git or Fossil can also retain detailed history. The extra requirement is to coordinate the exact states and dependencies that belong to a review. Gossil defines that coordination as part of its repository model, rather than leaving it to a convention between independent tools. Fossil already has immutable ticket artifacts and file history. The repository guide explains Gossil’s specified additions.

title: Compare Gossil with Git
text: Suppose an agent revises plan.md, marks its task ready for review, and saves a private trace of a failed approach. The implementation is in a separate Git repository. In the planned Gossil workflow: Review the plan diff, task changes and permitted evidence together. Request the integrated operation with the expected file and issue revisions. Record the Gossil artifacts, derived records, scope, local command history and checkout heads in one database transaction. Retain the permitted file head and the complete issue boundaries for later review. A file head identifies a file check-in. An issue boundary identifies its scope, complete contributing artifact set and projection version. Artifacts are immutable stored records; the projection version names the rules that reconstruct the issue’s values. Contributors include losing assignments even when a current screen displays other values. Notes, links and discussions need their required dependencies too. If the agent later changes only the task’s status, the file head stays the same. The earlier issue boundary still selects the state reviewed with the plan. Record-only changes create no file check-in. Later arrivals do not silently change that selected historical set, subject to permission and byte availability. A file hash alone cannot recover this context. The code link names a registered Git repository, full commit, path and blob, with a versioned selector when it names a range. The blob identifies file bytes. From the issue, a reviewer can reach the pinned code; from that code version, the reviewer can find the issue. A known filename or current checkout path helps locate material, but neither supplies its repository identity or historical version. Local paths can change without changing the registered repository’s identity. The design introduces no global file identity. Uncommitted code needs a captured snapshot. An authorized capture can retain bytes if the external Git checkout later disappears; an object reference alone does not guarantee availability. The link descriptor encoding remains unfinished. See the repository guide for the planned coordination and its limits. The integrated transaction commits changes to the Gossil database. An external Git commit remains a separate operation. Checkout files are written after database commit through recoverable work, so filesystem recovery can still be necessary. Ordinary issue edits do not automatically batch unrelated work.

title: Compare Gossil with Git
text: The planned Gossil checkout root can sit above several Git repositories. Select AGENTS.md and chosen agent files inside those repositories explicitly; initialization does not track every descendant. Gossil’s selection is independent of the nested Git indices and must preserve their branches and commits. The repository guide shows how to choose this layout. Git ignore rules help omit untracked files; they do not affect files already tracked. Sparse checkout controls which tracked paths appear in the working tree. Neither mechanism establishes a private/shared boundary for stored history. See gitignore and sparse checkout. Git transfer can select references through refspecs, which map source references to destinations. This selects history to fetch, not a confidentiality policy for individual paths. Access rules depend on the chosen repository and service configuration. See Git fetch. Gossil’s chosen design keeps private and shared history in one local repository. Shared history must be usable without private-only dependencies. Team replication, sync and autosync remain planned; this design does not promise arbitrary partial sharing within the shared portion today. This page follows the nossaifd writing guide, including principles credited to Rosalind Reid, Shreya Shankar and Oskar Austegard.

title: Compare Gossil with Git
text: Keep Git for source work today. Next, try the delta tutorial and use the repository guide to select agent files. For a future integrated review, retain the exact file head, complete issue boundaries and versioned code links together.

title: Library concepts
text: Gossil separates byte operations, artifact structure and local database ownership. A byte operation does not create a repository, and a parsed artifact does not establish its place in a repository graph. For file selection, check-ins, branches and sharing, read working with repositories. This page describes the library modules available to application authors.

title: Library concepts
section: Files and issues in one operation
text: The intended product coordinates agent files and structured issue records in one repository database. A local operation can commit a plan revision, its task change and a private trace together. Its transaction includes canonical artifacts, derived projections, scope, local command history and Gossil checkout heads. A projection is a database view of retained artifact records. Git remains the external source authority; its commits are separate operations. Checkout filesystem writes follow database commit through recoverable work. This integrated workflow remains planned. A historical view selects a permitted file check-in and exact record boundaries for each issue or discussion. The record boundary names the complete contributor set and projection version, with all dependencies required by the claimed view. Contributors are immutable artifacts that determine the record’s state. The projection version identifies the reconstruction rules; scope distinguishes shared access from an authorized owner’s combined view. Record-only changes create no file check-in, so a file hash alone cannot identify issue history. Later arrivals do not change the selected historical set. Access still depends on permission and byte availability. Typed links connect an issue to exact code versions and support reverse lookup from code to issues. A Git target pins its registered repository, commit, path and blob, with a versioned selector for a range. Captures can retain the permitted bytes; an object ID alone does not guarantee their availability. Shared history must be complete without private-only dependencies. Receiving it does not automatically update a checkout or an owner’s private issue selection. Explicit update and publication enforce the relevant revision and scope checks. A descriptor is a structured record naming a versioned link target and any selected range. Its transferable encoding remains unfinished, so these guides do not yet give a format that applications can exchange. Fossil supplies immutable file and ticket history; Gest supplies task workflows. Gossil’s specified additions coordinate exact issue boundaries with shared/private file heads and strengthen Gest’s multi-statement helpers with one owned transaction. Planned command undo validates complete inverse changes and rejects stale dependencies; it retains artifacts and does not rewind Git. Read compare Gossil with Git for the plan/task example and working with repositories for file selection. The library modules below provide the implemented subset.

title: Library concepts
text: The delta module creates and applies Fossil deltas. Application takes an explicit output limit. The compression module packs and unpacks blobs, which are stored byte sequences. Unpacking also takes a decoded size limit. The content_hash module computes content digests. A digest identifies bytes but does not grant access to them. The artifact_checksum module computes legacy MD5 checksums for artifact records. It does not choose the repository’s content hash policy.

title: Library concepts
text: The token_codec module escapes byte values for Fossil record tokens. Its byte and C-string forms have different zero-byte behavior. The token guide defines those contracts. The artifact module parses eight structural artifact types with explicit limits and checks their structure and checksums. A caller implements DateProvider, whose julianday method converts date fields to Julian day numbers. Repository graph validation requires more storage rules. See the parser guide.

title: Library concepts
text: LocalStore owns a local libSQL connection and one exclusive write transaction. A transaction must commit or roll back before the connection returns to the store. The public interface does not expose arbitrary SQL. LocalOwnerRepository initializes a complete empty public root. Its initialize constructor creates a repository without a checkout. The vcs init command calls this constructor, generates identities and a password, and selects a default administrator from the environment. The API requires those values explicitly. Its create constructor binds an existing checkout directory. Private content writes require the bound catalog1 repository and refuse the initializer-only catalog4 repository. The empty root is a check-in with no files. A private content write does not create a check-in that contains files. Admission is the validation of the stored root required before repository operations. SharedView restricts access to public content that passed this validation. Read and write access to the database file through the operating system establishes local owner authority. The native storage guide defines admission, content bounds and access rules. General links between artifacts in the repository graph remain planned, so parsing does not establish parent relationships or resolve references. Sync and team authentication also remain planned.

title: Library concepts
text: Gest is a task and artifact tracker. These converters use its task, project and author record model. The gest_task_values module validates eleven already decoded task fields. It returns an owned record with a standardized status and UTC timestamps. The task values guide defines validation and caller responsibilities. The gest_project_values module validates the four fields that make up the canonical Gest project record, gest_id, archived_at, created_at and updated_at. It returns an owned record with an identifier, nullable archive time and UTC timestamps. The project values guide defines the complete field contract. A local checkout root is outside the canonical project record. The gest_author_values module validates six canonical author fields and returns an owned record. It preserves names and nullable email exactly, normalizes author types and converts timestamps to UTC. The author values guide defines this conversion separately from native actors and local principals. The task ticket emitter produces bounded creation artifact bytes from a validated task, a separate native ticket identity, actor bytes and a typed UTC date. Before passing decoded task, project or author values to a converter, callers must check raw field presence, duplicates and byte limits. Storage integration and task, project or author commands remain separate work.

title: Inherited-test runner
text: gossil-conformance executes one Fossil Tcl suite against an explicit program. It is development infrastructure and implements no Gossil engine behavior. A reference run tests the pinned upstream Fossil program. A candidate run tests the replacement program whose compatibility is under development. The runs have separate configurations and output directories. A missing candidate never falls back to C Fossil. Run just conformance-self-test to check the runner controls. These tests pass when the runner correctly rejects deliberate failures and incomplete runs. That result does not mean the inherited Fossil suites pass.

title: Inherited-test runner
text: Install Rust with Cargo, Git, Just and uv on PATH before using the recipes. Rust builds the runner, Just runs Justfile recipes, and uv runs the installed workflow tools. just setup supplies the Linux reference tools and fetches Cargo dependencies. just install --check checks the saved workflow installation. The required references are Tcl 8.6.18 and Fossil 2.29 at revision 7e8ecf0ce4, with TLS and FUSE disabled. On Linux, just setup builds these tools from the archives pinned in evidence/reference-tools.json. It needs a C compiler, Make, zlib development headers and CA certificates. The Tcl installation retains its shell, shared library and core runtime scripts. Verified tools become available through ignored .jlog/bin links after the complete installation is published. Its receipt retains source identities, configure flags and binary hashes. Repeated setup checks and reuses that installation. Changed cache bytes and unknown tool paths fail without replacement. Worktrees can check and reuse shared managed references read-only when their source receipt, binary hashes and runtime observations match. On other hosts, setup checks and keeps the existing reference tools. Supply them before setup if they are absent. The current macOS tools remain the existing Tcl installation in Homebrew storage and the pinned local Fossil build. Setup does not adopt those external tools into its managed Linux installation. The read-only pull-request release check runs just setup before the full just check. Only a successful push to main can run its source-tag job. Local Linux native-tool controls and Python installer controls are separate from Rust coverage and the full Rust suite in CI. The bounded native setup receipt records the executed Linux scope.

title: Inherited-test runner
text: Write a JSON configuration with absolute paths. The following example uses the checked-in positive control. Replace /path/to/gossil with the checkout path. The output directory must not exist. Save this example as CONFIG.json. { "role": "reference", "revision": "b3a1c8efb2731dffbd5cc38c58ac349746de6da6", "tcl": "/path/to/gossil/.jlog/bin/tclsh", "driver": "/path/to/gossil/tests/fixtures/controls/tester.tcl", "executable": "/path/to/gossil/.jlog/bin/fossil", "suite": "pass", "run_dir": "/path/to/gossil/target/conformance/example", "timeout_ms": 3000, "seed": 20261117, "inputs": [ "/path/to/gossil/tests/fixtures/fossil/tester.tcl", "/path/to/gossil/tests/fixtures/fossil/enable.patch" ], "capabilities": {"tls": "disabled", "fuse": "disabled"} }

title: Inherited-test runner
text: Field Meaning and effect role Required label reference or candidate. It does not select a binary. revision Nonempty source identifier retained in evidence. The runner does not verify a source checkout against it. tcl Absolute path to an executable Tcl interpreter. driver Absolute path to the enabled tester.tcl driver. executable Absolute path to the program under test, used without fallback. suite Suite basename without a slash, for example pass for pass.test. run_dir Absolute path to a new output directory whose parent already exists. timeout_ms Positive deadline in milliseconds. A timeout rejects the run. seed Unsigned 32-bit value passed to Tcl srand before the driver runs. It controls Tcl randomness, not every source of randomness in the tested program. inputs Absolute paths to extra source, fixture or patch files whose bytes need hashing. capabilities Caller-supplied string map retained as evidence. It neither enables features nor verifies their availability. invocation_plan Optional complete plan and corpus pins; omitted or null uses strict duplicate-name rejection. See the plan contract below. The runner locates  .test beside driver. The example runs tests/fixtures/controls/pass.test. For an upstream suite, keep the original source tree and corpus unchanged. Put a copy of tester.tcl and the selected suite beside each other in a separate harness directory. Apply tests/fixtures/fossil/enable.patch only to the copied driver. text: The runner implements Unix process groups. The current checks ran on macOS, while Linux execution remains unqualified. Each invocation uses a fresh directory, a cleared environment, isolated HOME and temporary paths, and a fixed system utility PATH of /usr/bin:/bin. The runner observes completion without reaping the process-group leader. It checks the group identity before terminating owned descendants, then reaps the direct child. A timeout always rejects the run. Execution assumes trusted local programs with the same user credentials. The runner rejects setuid and setgid targets. Descendants that change their credentials, process group or session are unsupported. The runner is not a sandbox and does not promise a deadline for uninterruptible kernel work. It reaps its direct child and terminates descendants in the same process group. On macOS, XNU returns EPERM for a group containing only zombies. After the leader exits, the runner records that outcome as no-signalable-members under the trusted-program assumptions above. Other permission failures block the run. The XNU signal implementation defines that behavior.

title: Bounded delta decoder
text: API: apply gives the exact contract. gossil::delta applies Fossil deltas to byte slices. A delta describes output with literal bytes and copies from an original byte slice. The library validates the commands before allocating output, then returns the decoded bytes. The gossil vcs test-delta-apply diagnostic exposes that decoder through files. It opens no repository or database and does not forward work to C Fossil.

title: Bounded delta decoder
text: From the repository root, run: cargo run --locked --bin gossil -- vcs test-delta-apply ORIGIN DELTA TARGET Replace ORIGIN, DELTA and TARGET with file paths. Quote paths that contain spaces. The command reads both inputs and finishes decoding before it opens TARGET. The target can be the same path as either input. On success, it writes exactly the decoded bytes, returns status 0 and leaves stdout and stderr empty. Cargo may print build messages on stderr before the executable runs. The command returns status 1 for usage, read, decode, allocation or write errors. The characterized diagnostics are: Failure Stderr line Unsupported command or argument count Usage: gossil vcs test-delta-apply ORIGIN DELTA TARGET Missing input no such file: PATH Delta rejection or buffer reservation failure Delta application failed. Target open or write failure unable to open file "PATH" for writing Each diagnostic ends with one LF byte, and stdout remains empty. Other input read errors include the path and the underlying I/O error. The command has no root-level test-delta-apply alias. Usage, input-read and decode failures preserve an existing target because it has not been opened. A write failure can leave a truncated or partially written target. The command does not replace files atomically.

title: Bounded delta decoder
text: The decoder API exposes output_size, apply, Limits and DeltaError. The same module also exposes the encoder function create. output_size(delta) parses only the advertised output size and its LF delimiter. It does not validate the commands or enforce the output limit used by apply. use gossil::delta::{Limits, apply, output_size}; let delta = b"3\n3:ABC0;"; assert_eq!(output_size(delta).unwrap(), 3); let output = apply(b"", delta, Limits { max_output_bytes: 1024 }).unwrap(); assert_eq!(output, b"ABC"); apply(source, delta, limits) returns Result , DeltaError>. The result has exactly the advertised size, with no trailing NUL byte. Both input slices must fit within i32::MAX bytes. The output ceiling is the smaller of limits.max_output_bytes and i32::MAX. Limits::default() uses i32::MAX, as does the file diagnostic. The first pass checks command syntax, source ranges, literal lengths, cumulative output length and the final size. After validation, the decoder reserves output storage with a fallible operation and replays the checked slices in a second pass. It stores no list of parsed operations. Invalid commands reach no output reservation. An empty result needs no reservation. The decoder returns these DeltaError variants: Error variant Meaning MissingHeaderNewline Header digits are not followed by LF. InputTooLarge A source or delta input exceeds the signed-length envelope. OutputTooLarge The advertised output exceeds the effective ceiling. TruncatedCommand A numeric command has no following operator. MissingCopyComma A copy offset has no present comma delimiter. UnknownOperator An operator byte is not defined. SourceRange A copy exceeds the source, including a zero copy beyond its end. OutputRange A command would exceed the advertised output. TruncatedLiteral A literal has fewer bytes than its count. Unterminated The input ends or reaches a command-start NUL before a semicolon. SizeMismatch A semicolon arrives before the advertised output is complete. AllocationFailed Output reservation failed, with the original TryReserveError retained as its cause. Fallible reservation reports recoverable allocation failures. It does not guarantee recovery from an operating-system kill or memory exhaustion after a successful reservation.

title: Bounded delta decoder
text: A delta starts with the encoded output length and LF. The form COUNT:BYTES inserts a literal, COUNT@OFFSET, copies from the source, and CHECKSUM; ends the delta. All numbers use the alphabet below. The decoder uses the exact unsigned-byte digit alphabet: 0123456789ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ_abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz~ Numbers wrap modulo 2^32, and empty numeric fields mean zero. High-bit bytes are not aliases for ASCII digits or delimiters. Zero-count copies still require a valid source offset and a comma. Literal payloads can contain arbitrary bytes. The decoder requires a semicolon and an exact final output size, then ignores trailing bytes. Checksum verification is disabled, as it is in the pinned reference build. The numeric field before the semicolon is parsed but not checked against the output. Accepted wrong-checksum fixtures remain accepted. Checked ranges and slice access reject truncation at boundaries where the C implementation can read beyond its logical input. Those C pointer behaviors are not format guarantees.

title: Bounded delta encoder
text: From the repository root, replace the capitalized arguments with file paths: cargo run --locked --bin gossil -- vcs test-delta-create ORIGIN TARGET DELTA cargo run --locked --bin gossil -- vcs test-delta FILE1 FILE2 test-delta-create reads both inputs before opening DELTA for writing. The output can share either input path. Success returns status 0 with empty stdout and stderr. test-delta creates and applies deltas in both directions, compares both results with the original bytes, and prints ok followed by LF. A failed comparison, creation or round-trip application returns status 1 with delta test failed on stderr. File-buffer reservation failures return Delta application failed.. Cargo may print build messages on stderr before the executable runs. The commands require exactly three and two paths, respectively. Usage errors return status 1 and the matching usage line. Missing inputs produce no such file: PATH. Output failures produce unable to open file "PATH" for writing. Each diagnostic ends with LF. Other read errors retain the path and underlying I/O error. Usage and input-read failures preserve an existing output. Writing can truncate an existing output before a later write fails. These diagnostics have no root command aliases. They read and write file data through paths. test-delta uses stdout only for its ok diagnostic. Reading file data from stdin, writing file data to stdout, automatic parent-folder creation and complete native I/O diagnostic parity are outside this qualification.

title: Bounded delta encoder
text: The encoder follows the pinned Fossil src/delta.c algorithm. It indexes source landmarks, scans target windows for matching source bytes, and emits copies when they cover their encoding overhead. Other bytes become literals. Its rolling hash uses sixteen signed bytes, matching the selected native build. Checksums sum unsigned big-endian four-byte words with wrapping arithmetic and right-zero padding for the last short word. Sources of at most sixteen bytes produce one literal, including a zero-length literal for an empty target. Longer sources omit that zero literal. The hash tables omit the last complete source block and visit newer landmarks first. Each target window examines at most 250 candidates. Backward extension stops before source offset zero. A match equal to its encoding overhead is accepted. Equal-length candidates retain the first visited match, and the first target window with a winning match emits it immediately. Both inputs must fit within i32::MAX bytes. The encoder counts integer digits with unsigned arithmetic. The native signed shift above 2^30 is undefined. Unsigned counting there is a safe Rust policy and does not promise giant-input native parity. Slice lengths and addresses remain bounded by existing inputs. Every output append reserves storage before extending the vector. Both hash tables also reserve before initialization. EncoderAllocationFailed records the buffer stage, requested element count and original TryReserveError cause. The source and target size checks reuse InputTooLarge. Tests exercise genuine capacity-overflow errors without asking the allocator for giant storage. Fallible reservation does not promise recovery from an operating-system kill.

title: Compare normalized byte lines
text: The diff module compares two byte slices and returns an edit script in line counts. Use line_diff(from, to, options, limits) when a caller needs Fossil’s line matching and edit ordering without a rendered patch. Bytes need not be valid UTF-8. The module opens no files or databases. Normalize the input before calling this API. Fossil’s full text_diff wrapper uses blob_to_utf8_no_bom to remove a byte order mark or convert UTF-16. This module does neither. It also supplies no token diff, regular expression filter or text renderer. Its results describe the supplied bytes, after the caller’s chosen conversion.

title: Compare normalized byte lines
text: line_diff returns Result , DiffError>. Each Edit has three counts: Field Lines consumed copy Common lines from both inputs. delete Lines from FROM only. insert Lines from TO only. Read each triple in that order. Advance FROM by copy + delete and TO by copy + insert. The vector ends with the native zero triple, whose three counts are zero. Inserted content comes from TO. The script holds counts and omits line bytes. LF separates lines and is excluded from comparison. An unterminated final line still counts as a line. Adding or removing its final LF alone produces no line change. An empty input has zero lines.

title: Compare normalized byte lines
text: LineDiffOptions::default() selects exact comparison, native readability optimization and no other option. Choose these fields for each call: Field Behavior whitespace: Whitespace::Exact Compare all bytes within a line. whitespace: Whitespace::IgnoreEol Ignore trailing Fossil whitespace bytes. whitespace: Whitespace::IgnoreAll Ignore Fossil whitespace throughout a line. strip_cr Remove a trailing CR from each line before comparison. invert Exchange FROM and TO before computing edits. optimize Apply native readability shifts to insertions and deletions. not_too_big Reject more than 10,000 inserted plus deleted lines. Fossil whitespace here means bytes 8, 9, 10, 12, 13 and 32. It is not Unicode whitespace. IgnoreEol and IgnoreAll return the error DiffError::WhitespaceOnly when the script has one copy-only triple followed by the zero triple. They can also return scripts that contain edits.

title: Compare normalized byte lines
text: DiffLimits::default() supplies finite bounds. Applications can choose smaller bounds for their inputs: Field Default and meaning max_input_bytes 16 MiB combined input bytes. max_lines 200,000 combined input lines. max_edits 200,001 triples, including the final zero triple. max_work 100,000,000 charged inspections, comparisons and search iterations. The implementation also caps combined bytes at i32::MAX and combined lines at 1,000,000, even when caller limits are larger. Work is a charged algorithm budget. It does not measure each processor instruction or total heap bytes. Input bounds are checked before line-table allocation, and reservations can fail. DiffError::Binary reports an embedded NUL or a line longer than 32,767 bytes. WhitespaceOnly reports the rejection described above for the whitespace modes. TooManyChanges reports the enabled change-count rejection. Limit reports a caller bound or fixed cap, checked arithmetic failure or allocation failure. A failure returns no partial script.

title: Gest author values
text: The gossil::gest_author_values module validates all six canonical author fields in memory. Use it for complete decoded snapshots before storage integration. Gest is a task and artifact tracker. An author record identifies a human or agent in its record model. Accepting the human value here does not deliver native Human workflows. AuthorValueInputs requires an explicit serde_json::Value for gest_id, author_type, name, email, created_at and updated_at. author_from_values returns an AuthorValues record with private fields. author_to_values returns all six fields as independent owned values. See library setup for Cargo dependencies.

title: Gest author values
text: Before decoding raw input, check required fields, unknown fields and duplicate keys. Decoding can collapse duplicate keys. Then supply every field, including an explicit null for absent email. use gossil::gest_author_values::{AuthorValueInputs, author_from_values, author_to_values}; use serde_json::json; let author = author_from_values(AuthorValueInputs { gest_id: json!("kkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkk"), author_type: json!("AGENT"), name: json!(" Alice "), email: json!(null), created_at: json!("2026-11-19T01:02:03.000000001+02:00"), updated_at: json!("2020-01-01T00:00:00Z"), }).unwrap(); let values = author_to_values(&author); assert_eq!(values.author_type, json!("agent")); assert_eq!(values.name, json!(" Alice ")); assert_eq!(values.email, json!(null)); assert_eq!(values.created_at, json!("2026-11-18T23:02:03.000000001+00:00")); assert_eq!(author_from_values(values).unwrap(), author); The modification time precedes creation in this example because conversion imposes no time ordering. It generates no identity or time and performs no SQL.

title: Gest author values
text: The identifier must contain exactly 32 lowercase letters from k through z. The author type accepts case-insensitive human or agent and emits lowercase. It rejects surrounding whitespace and other values. Names accept any string, including empty strings, whitespace and control characters. Email accepts an explicit null or any string. Null and an empty string remain distinct. Conversion does not check email syntax or trim either field. Both timestamps require strings that chrono 0.4.44 can parse as RFC3339. Conversion normalizes each instant to UTC and checks that its output can be parsed again. It rejects output outside that canonical RFC3339 domain. AuthorValueError displays the field and a static reason without echoing input. Its parse_cause() accessor returns the actual chrono error from input parsing or canonical output parsing. Other failures have no parser cause.

title: Gest author values
text: Callers own raw decoding, field admission, duplicate detection, byte limits, reference checks and the history of changes to the record. An author record is separate from native actor bytes and local principals. Conversion does not establish uniqueness, authorization, storage, lifecycle, replay, migration or the complete Gest API. The seven controls in tests/gest_author_values.rs cover field types, identifiers, author types, exact strings, nullable email, timestamps, parser causes and owned output. These controls exercise the pure converter. They do not test storage or native workflows. Their presence does not establish an executed test pass.

title: Gest project values
text: The gossil::gest_project_values module converts all four canonical project fields into an owned, validated record. Use it for complete decoded snapshots before storage integration. Project persistence and CLI commands remain planned. Gest is a task and artifact tracker. These converters use its task and project record model. A Gest project represents a tracked repository or directory. Here, canonical means the four project fields in the reviewed field map. In a source checkout, the map is tests/fixtures/gest_project_values/source-map.json. ProjectValueInputs requires an explicit serde_json::Value for gest_id, archived_at, created_at and updated_at. project_from_values returns a ProjectValues record with private fields. project_to_values returns all four fields as independent owned values. The local checkout root is a filesystem path and is not canonical data. The upstream project model defines the source record. See library setup for Cargo dependencies.

title: Gest project values
text: Before constructing serde_json::Value inputs, callers check raw JSON for required fields, unknown fields and duplicate keys. Duplicate keys must be checked before decoding collapses them. Then assemble every field for conversion. Nullable archive state requires an explicit null. The converter does not read a clock, generate an identifier, look up references or execute SQL. use gossil::gest_project_values::{ProjectValueInputs, project_from_values, project_to_values}; use serde_json::json; let fields = ProjectValueInputs { gest_id: json!("kkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkk"), archived_at: json!(null), created_at: json!("2026-11-18T07:00:00-05:00"), updated_at: json!("2025-01-01T00:00:00Z"), }; let project = project_from_values(fields).unwrap(); let values = project_to_values(&project); assert_eq!(values.created_at, json!("2026-11-18T12:00:00+00:00")); assert_eq!(project_from_values(values).unwrap(), project); The example sets modification before creation to show that conversion imposes no time ordering.

title: Gest project values
text: The identifier must contain exactly 32 lowercase letters from k through z. Archive state accepts null or an RFC3339 timestamp. Creation and modification timestamps require strings. Shared validation uses chrono 0.4.44, normalizes to UTC and checks that the output can be parsed again. It imposes no time ordering. ProjectValueError displays the field and a static reason without echoing input. Its parse_cause() accessor retains the actual chrono error from input parsing or canonical UTC output parsing. Other failures have no parser cause. Callers own raw decoding, required-field presence, unknown-field classification, duplicate keys in the original input, byte budgets and reference checks. Callers also check the complete history of changes to the record. The converter does not establish project uniqueness or implement lifecycle, replay, migration, storage or the complete Gest API.

title: Gest project values
text: The seven converter controls in tests/gest_project_values.rs check complete output, independent ownership, types, identifiers, nullable archive state and timestamp boundaries with typed causes. These tests cover the converter itself. They do not reproduce the upstream project API or repository tests, whose behavior and persistence still need separate validation. The project fixtures retain the reviewed field map and frozen catalog source provenance in tests/fixtures/gest_catalog_values/source-map.json. The broader map does not imply that other catalog models ship here. Project storage and reads of caller-selected records remain planned through the repository transaction API.

title: Gest task values
text: The gossil::gest_task_values module converts eleven already decoded task fields into an owned, validated record. Callers can use the record for complete task snapshots before storage integration. Pass validated snapshots to the task ticket emitter for bounded creation artifact bytes. The module does not implement the full Gest API or migrate stored repositories. Gest is a task and artifact tracker. This converter uses its task record model. Here, canonical values use the status and UTC timestamp forms defined below. TaskValueInputs requires an explicit serde_json::Value for each field. task_from_values validates these values and returns TaskValues, whose fields are private. task_to_values returns the complete set of owned values. The functions do not read a clock, generate identifiers or execute SQL.

title: Gest task values
text: Check raw input field presence, duplicates and byte limits before assembling decoded values. No field has a default. The public input and output use the same TaskValueInputs type. use gossil::gest_task_values::{TaskValueInputs, task_from_values, task_to_values}; use serde_json::json; let fields = TaskValueInputs { gest_id: json!("zyxwvutsrqponmlkzyxwvutsrqponmlk"), project_id: json!("kkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkk"), title: json!("Review task values"), priority: json!(255), status: json!("IN_PROGRESS"), description: json!(""), assigned_to: json!(null), metadata: json!([null, {"reviewed": false}]), resolved_at: json!(null), created_at: json!("2026-11-18T07:00:00-05:00"), updated_at: json!("2026-11-18T12:00:00Z"), }; let task = task_from_values(fields).unwrap(); let values = task_to_values(&task); assert_eq!(values.status, json!("in-progress")); assert_eq!(values.created_at, json!("2026-11-18T12:00:00+00:00")); assert_eq!(task_from_values(values).unwrap(), task); The example uses array metadata and priority 255 to show the model’s full value types. Production callers must handle TaskValueError from validation. Its display text names the first rejected field and the reason, without echoing the supplied value. TaskValueError::parse_cause() returns the original chrono::ParseError when parsing the input or its canonical UTC output fails. Callers can inspect its kind() to distinguish failures such as TooShort and OutOfRange. Other validation failures return no parse cause. Error equality includes the retained cause, so errors with equal display text can compare unequal. Chrono’s alloc-only build does not implement std::error::Error for this parser error, so callers use the accessor rather than Error::source(). The validated record stays unchanged if a caller changes the owned fields returned by task_to_values.

title: Gest task values
text: The input requires all eleven fields, even when a value is null. Field Admitted value gest_id Full task ID string, called id in Gest’s task Model. project_id Full project ID string. title Any string. priority Null or a JSON integer from 0 through 255. status A status string accepted by Gest’s task status FromStr implementation. description Any string. assigned_to Null or a full author ID string. metadata Any serde_json::Value, including null. resolved_at A timestamp string for terminal status, otherwise null. created_at A timestamp string. updated_at A timestamp string. The task and project identifiers require exactly 32 lowercase letters from k through z. An assignee is null or a full identifier. Title and description preserve their strings, including empty strings, Unicode, whitespace and null characters. The task field gest_id corresponds to upstream Model.id. Priority is null or an integer from 0 through 255. Checked conversion rejects negative integers, larger integers, floating point values and other JSON types. The upstream task model uses Option . Its separate named priority enum covers only 0 through 4 and is outside this module. Status parsing follows upstream FromStr. The statuses are open, in-progress, done and cancelled. Parsing accepts case differences and the in-progress, in_progress and inprogress aliases. Output uses in-progress. The adopted Gossil contract requires a resolution timestamp for done and cancelled, and null for open and in-progress. The converter checks that pairing without generating a timestamp. Metadata retains every JSON value variant, including null. Explicit metadata null is model data, independent of the nulls in optional model fields. The converter preserves JSON value semantics without promising original JSON spelling, object member order or duplicate-key detection. Business timestamps use Gest’s pinned chrono 0.4.44 RFC3339 parser and normalize to Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), subject to Gossil’s canonical output contract. RFC3339 is the timestamp string format used at this boundary. Output uses chrono’s RFC3339 form with the +00:00 offset and at most nine fractional digits. The parser accepts offsets, lowercase separators, a space separator, year zero and leap seconds. It truncates fractional input beyond nanoseconds, as upstream does. Business timestamp rules are separate from the stricter artifact D-card time grammar. The converter adds no ordering rule between timestamps. A parsed instant must have a UTC representation that the RFC3339 parser can read back. Offset normalization across the year zero or 9999 boundary can produce a signed extended year. The converter rejects those results under the adopted output contract. Upstream source parsing accepts their inputs. Year zero and nearby offsets remain valid when their UTC result is representable. The module does not claim parity with the full upstream timestamp input domain. Invalid field types, incomplete identifiers, invalid priorities or statuses, unparseable timestamps and inconsistent status/resolution pairs return TaskValueError. Normalized UTC output outside the adopted RFC3339 domain also returns that error. Metadata has no further type restriction.

title: Gest task values
text: Cargo.toml pins chrono to 0.4.44 with default features disabled and alloc as its only enabled feature. Clock access and chrono’s serde support are disabled. The lockfile includes chrono 0.4.44, num-traits 0.2.19 and autocfg 1.5.1. These additions support timestamp conversion in Rust and do not add a native Fossil process or a SQL date conversion to this module.

title: Gest task values
text: The caller must validate and decode raw fields before constructing the input. For ticket artifacts, it must classify each J card, which assigns a named field. It must check complete field presence, reject duplicate field spellings where required and enforce byte limits for the operation. The explicit input struct is not an object decoder and cannot identify fields that the caller discarded. The enclosing implementation must validate history, resolve references to other records and decide which unsupported fields or records to reject. This module supplies complete task values for before and after snapshots. The separate task ticket emitter supplies creation bytes. Applying history, recording operation recipes and the source of changes, undoing operations and writing storage remain separate work. The converter does not enable migration of stored repositories.

title: Get started
text: Use Gossil to create a delta between two files and restore the target exactly. A delta encodes target bytes as new bytes and copies from an origin file. This exercise needs no repository and does not change Git history. Gossil is intended to keep agent files, issues and their history alongside Git. Its command line initializes empty repositories and has three delta diagnostics. The Rust library also supports artifact parsing, local storage and task, project and author value conversion. Try the delta commands below. Read working with repositories for the intended file and issue workflows.

title: Get started
text: Install Git, Rust with Cargo, Just, uv and the jlog command recorder. These tools must be available on PATH. Rust builds also need the native compiler and platform development tools used by Cargo dependencies. Linux setup also requires Make, zlib development headers and CA certificates to build the pinned Tcl and Fossil references. On other hosts, supply the reference prerequisites before setup. The commands below use a POSIX shell, such as the default shell on macOS or Linux. git clone https://github.com/rahuldave/gossil.git cd gossil just setup just setup supplies the Linux references or checks the existing tools on other hosts, then fetches the Cargo dependencies. just gossil then builds and runs the source executable through jlog and Cargo. You do not need a globally installed gossil executable. The first build can take longer than later calls. The example builds from source. Keep the checkout open in this shell for the following commands. The contributor setup is for people who also need the optional workflow packages and verification guidance.

title: Get started
text: Make a fresh scratch folder so that the example cannot overwrite earlier work. Keep the quotation marks around paths so that paths with spaces work too. example_dir=$(mktemp -d /tmp/gossil-example.XXXXXX) printf 'before\n' > "$example_dir/origin" printf 'after\n' > "$example_dir/target" just gossil vcs test-delta-create "$example_dir/origin" "$example_dir/target" "$example_dir/change.delta" The arguments are the original file, the desired file, and the delta to write. Success writes change.delta and prints no command output. Cargo can print build messages on stderr. A delta need not be smaller than its target, especially for small files like these.

title: Get started
text: Apply the delta to the same origin, writing a separate restored file: just gossil vcs test-delta-apply "$example_dir/origin" "$example_dir/change.delta" "$example_dir/restored" cmp "$example_dir/target" "$example_dir/restored" cat "$example_dir/restored" cmp prints nothing and exits with status 0 when the files match. cat prints after. The original and target files remain available. To check that Gossil can create and apply deltas in both directions, run: just gossil vcs test-delta "$example_dir/origin" "$example_dir/target" Success prints ok. This command checks the round trip in memory. It does not save another delta or create a check-in. You can repeat these commands with text or binary files. A delta describes bytes, so keep its matching origin when you need to restore the target later.

title: Get started
text: v is the short name for vcs: just gossil v test-delta "$example_dir/origin" "$example_dir/target" The source also builds a gos executable with the same diagnostics. See short executable names for its source invocation. These aliases do not enable issue, checkout or sync commands.

title: Get started
section: Handle failures and choose the next step
text: A diagnostic exits with status 1 and writes an error to stderr when it fails. Check the input paths and argument order first. If applying a delta fails, check that you kept the correct origin and an intact delta. The CLI reference lists the exact messages. Successful create and apply operations replace an existing output file. Use a fresh output path until you have checked the result. Validation failures preserve the output, but a write failure can leave it truncated. The repository guide explains how a file delta differs from a check-in and how Gossil is intended to work beside Git. For application code, use the library examples and generated Rust API. The application manifest must select Gossil’s bundled libSQL provider as shown in those examples. The provider implements the Fossil date arithmetic required by artifact parsing and repository validation.

title: Get started
text: Choose a destination that does not exist: just gossil vcs init --admin-user alice example.gossil The receipt gives the project and server identifiers and the initial administrator password. Save the password privately. This command creates the empty root without a checkout or tracked files. It reads no preference file. See the initialization reference for date, hash and login options. The existing default mini-VCS preview is a separate installation; these commands build the current source.

title: Get started

title: Gossil
text: Gossil aims to keep agent work, issues and file history together alongside Git. Fossil is a version-control system. This build exposes a Rust library for its delta bytes, artifact parsing and local storage. The gossil command creates, applies and checks deltas between files without a version-control checkout. It also initializes an empty repository through vcs init, without creating a checkout. Start with a file round trip, browse the CLI reference, or use the Rust API reference. Use working with repositories to plan agent files alongside Git. It explains checkouts, stored history and the intended private and shared workflows. For an already installed development preview, try the disposable file-history walkthrough. The preview is unmerged. Read compare Gossil with Git for the planned coordination of file history, exact issue state and versioned links to code. The examples show library calls for deltas, compressed bytes, hashes and token escaping. Gest is a task and artifact tracker. The converters in the module table use its task, project and author record model.
